title: Sentinel, Defender XDR, and the security data platform
subtitle: Choose the right layer for ingestion, detection, investigation, and historical analysis.
intro: SC-200 scenarios often describe a requirement rather than name the feature that satisfies it. Start by drawing a data path: source, ingestion, table, detection, incident, response. Microsoft Sentinel supplies SIEM coverage for Microsoft, third-party, cloud, and on-premises sources. Defender XDR correlates signals from deployed Defender workloads. The Defender portal brings those workflows together, while the Sentinel data lake adds economical historical analysis and graph capabilities. A unified screen does not remove the need to configure connectors, permissions, tables, and response resources. Learn what each layer contributes so you can identify the missing prerequisite instead of choosing a familiar product name.

sections.title: Build the operational path
sections.body: A Log Analytics workspace becomes a Sentinel workspace when Sentinel is enabled on it. Start with the workspace region, access model, retention needs, and data sources. A connector makes a supported source available, but the source may still need diagnostic settings, an agent, API credentials, or collection configuration. Inspect the connector instructions and destination tables. An installed solution packages useful content; it does not prove telemetry is arriving. For a firewall investigation, verify actual recent records before enabling a detection that expects them. A successful deployment and a successful data flow are different checkpoints.

sections.title: Use the unified portal deliberately
sections.body: Connecting Sentinel workspaces to the Defender portal enables combined incident handling and hunting with Defender XDR where those services are deployed. A tenant can have a primary Sentinel workspace and connected secondary workspaces. Select the intended workspace and check its connection state when a feature appears empty. Portal access does not itself grant every Azure or Defender permission. Sentinel can be used in the Defender portal without purchasing an XDR license simply for that portal experience. Product-specific telemetry and response actions still depend on their own deployment, licensing, configuration, and permissions.

sections.title: Understand the lake and graph layer
sections.body: The Sentinel data lake separates long-term storage from the compute used to analyze it. Analytics data supports operational detection and interactive investigation; lake-only data serves historical analysis through the supported lake query, job, and notebook experiences. Graph uses relationships and asset context to help investigate connected risk. Onboarding requires a connected primary workspace and appropriate setup roles; choose the supported region and billing resources carefully. For the exam, distinguish adding a workspace to the portal from completing lake onboarding. Neither operation magically supplies missing endpoint, identity, or third-party telemetry.

sections.title: Move from content to validated capability
sections.body: Content hub is the starting point for packaged connectors, workbook templates, analytics templates, and automation content. Install the relevant solution, configure its connector, validate tables, and then create active content from templates. Templates require adaptation to your environment, including entity mapping and exceptions. Track updates and verify that customizations still behave correctly. When a scenario says an analyst installed a solution but has no incidents, ask whether data arrived, the rule was activated, its query returned results, and its incident settings permit incident creation. This sequence is more reliable than reinstalling everything.

remember: Sentinel workspace, Defender portal connection, and lake onboarding are distinct steps.
A content template is not necessarily an active rule or saved workbook.
A unified portal still uses the permissions and deployment prerequisites of underlying products.
pitfalls: Do not assume Defender XDR automatically collects every third-party log.
Do not assume lake-only storage supports every real-time SIEM feature.

title: Sentinel RBAC and playbook permissions
subtitle: Separate analyst access, engineering rights, workflow authoring, and service execution.
intro: Permission questions become manageable when you identify the actor, action, resource, and scope. Reading an incident, changing a rule, editing a Logic App, and letting Sentinel invoke a playbook are separate operations. A role that is sufficient for one need might intentionally omit another. SC-200 expects you to choose a workable combination with limited privilege and to diagnose why an existing assignment fails. Also distinguish Azure RBAC on the SIEM workspace from Microsoft Entra and Defender permission models used by the wider platform. A person’s permissions are not automatically the permissions of Sentinel’s service identity or a playbook’s managed identity.

sections.title: Assign analyst and engineer roles
sections.body: Sentinel Reader supports viewing Sentinel resources and data. Responder adds incident management, such as assignment and status changes. Contributor adds creation and editing of Sentinel resources such as analytics rules and content management. Choose the least powerful role that supports the actual task. A triage analyst who must resolve incidents generally needs Responder rather than Reader; an engineer editing detections needs Contributor. Role scope matters as much as the name. Resource-group assignments commonly cover the workspace and associated resources more predictably than assigning permissions to a single object and overlooking related resources.

sections.title: Keep workflow authority separate
sections.body: Playbooks are Azure Logic Apps resources. Sentinel Contributor does not, by itself, grant Logic Apps authoring rights. Use Logic App Contributor when a person must create or modify the workflow. A person who only lists and manually runs playbooks can use Sentinel Playbook Operator alongside the access needed to open the incident. When a run is unavailable, verify the workflow trigger, location, and permissions rather than adding subscription Owner reflexively. An account can have enough authority to change an incident while having no authority to edit the workflow attached to it. These Logic App Contributor examples apply to Consumption playbooks; Standard workflows use the corresponding Logic Apps Standard Developer, Operator, or Contributor roles for their required operations.

sections.title: Check service and connector identities
sections.body: Sentinel uses its own service account to execute incident playbooks. That identity needs Sentinel Automation Contributor on the resource group containing the playbook. An administrator with role-assignment authority grants this access; granting the human Contributor on the workspace does not substitute for it. The workflow then calls target systems through connector connections or managed identities, which need their own target permissions. For example, permission to start an enrichment workflow does not automatically authorize its identity to read secrets. Troubleshoot execution permission and downstream API authorization as separate stages in run history.

sections.title: Understand scope and cumulative access
sections.body: Azure role assignments are additive. Assigning Reader cannot reduce rights inherited from Contributor at a parent scope. Review inherited assignments when access appears broader than intended. For workspace logs, distinguish workspace-wide access from supported resource-context access and table controls. Lake-wide roles can be broader than a workspace-only analyst requires; the current platform supports scoped workspace read access and separate system-table permissions. Ask which workspace, data collection, or resource the person needs before choosing a role. For an exam scenario, a correct role at the wrong scope is still an incomplete configuration.

Logic App Contributor is for workflow authoring; Playbook Operator supports manual execution.
Sentinel’s service identity needs Automation Contributor on the playbook resource group.
Inherited Azure RBAC permissions are cumulative.

A workflow’s downstream connector authorization is separate from permission to start it.

title: Windows Security Events, AMA, and WEF
subtitle: Select the collection path, DCR, and destination table your detections actually need.
intro: An empty Windows detection is frequently an ingestion or table mismatch rather than a faulty query. Windows Security Events via Azure Monitor Agent writes security events to SecurityEvent. Windows Event Forwarding centralizes selected events at a Windows Event Collector, where AMA can ingest them through the Windows Forwarded Events connector into WindowsEvent. Generic Azure Monitor Windows event collection can use Event instead. These distinctions are exam-relevant because many built-in Sentinel rules query a specific table. Learn the collection path, the association that targets machines, the event filter, and the table schema before tuning a threshold or assuming forwarding failed.

sections.title: Choose direct AMA collection
sections.body: Use the Windows Security Events via AMA connector when machines can run the supported agent and you want Sentinel’s SecurityEvent-oriented security content. Non-Azure servers generally need Azure Arc integration for this extension-based collection path. A data collection rule defines what to collect and the workspace destination. A data collection rule association determines which machines use the rule. Installing an agent alone does not mean that the intended DCR applies. Validate the machine identity, association, event generation, network access, and destination before concluding that Sentinel is dropping an event.

sections.title: Filter events where it makes sense
sections.body: Common, Minimal, All, and custom selections represent different coverage and volume decisions. Minimal is not a promise of a complete audit trail. With custom XPath, choose the correct channel and event identifiers; test the expression against actual event data. An event filter cannot create records that audit policy never generates on the source. Align the selected event set with the analytics templates and investigation requirements. For example, excluding logon failure records undermines a password-spray use case even if the agent and workspace connection are healthy. Reducing ingestion should preserve the evidence your detections need.

sections.title: Plan WEF and WEC as a separate hop
sections.body: WEF forwards selected source events to a Windows Event Collector. Source-initiated subscriptions can be distributed through Group Policy, and source audit policy and channel access must permit the expected collection. The collector runs the Windows Event Collection service and AMA for the Sentinel connection. This architecture can meet a requirement that individual sources cannot each host the monitoring agent. Check both hops: source to WEC, then WEC to Azure. Seeing events on the collector proves only the first hop. Examine collector capacity, subscription health, and the DCR when planning scale or troubleshooting missing data.

sections.title: Validate the correct table and fields
sections.body: The Windows Forwarded Events connector stores events in WindowsEvent, including forwarded Security-channel events. It does not automatically populate SecurityEvent. A built-in rule reading SecurityEvent therefore needs a compatible ingestion path or an adapted query and mapping. Generic Azure Monitor event collection can instead populate Event. Query recent counts by computer and event identifier, inspect a sample event, and check the timestamps. Schema-aware parsers help normalize fields across sources, but a parser is not a forwarding configuration. Always match the connector’s destination schema with the detection query before enabling production alerting.

pitfalls: Events visible at WEC do not prove ingestion to Sentinel.

title: Syslog and CEF through Azure Monitor Agent
subtitle: Trace appliance logs through a Linux forwarder, DCR filtering, and the right table.
intro: Network appliances often cannot run AMA themselves. A Linux forwarder receives their Syslog traffic, and AMA sends selected messages onward to the workspace. CEF adds a structured event format on top of the transport so Sentinel can populate normalized CommonSecurityLog fields; ordinary Syslog commonly lands in Syslog. SC-200 can test connector choice, forwarding prerequisites, filtering, duplicate ingestion, and failure isolation. Follow the message through each boundary instead of assuming that an open network port proves the entire integration works. Source formatting, local daemon behavior, rule association, facility and severity selection, and cloud connectivity can each break a different part of the path.

sections.title: Select format and collector architecture
sections.body: Syslog is the transport and message ecosystem; CEF is a security event format that can be carried by Syslog. A CEF header identifies vendor, product, event class, and severity, followed by extension fields. Use the CEF via AMA connector for compatible security appliance output and expect CommonSecurityLog. Use Syslog via AMA for ordinary Syslog and expect Syslog. The forwarder is a supported Linux machine with rsyslog or syslog-ng and AMA. When it is outside Azure, check the Azure Arc prerequisite. Install the relevant solution and follow the vendor’s appliance configuration instructions.

sections.title: Configure both network boundaries
sections.body: The appliance sends to the Linux daemon’s configured listening address, port, and transport. The daemon then forwards selected messages to AMA, which uses outbound connectivity to Azure. These are different connections; allowing appliance traffic alone does not authorize cloud egress. Confirm the daemon is listening on the interface that the appliance can reach, and verify actual received messages with an approved test or packet capture. Then verify the daemon-to-agent handoff and agent health. Use the documented current agent configuration rather than assuming a port from an older blog still applies.

sections.title: Make the DCR match the intended logs
sections.body: A data collection rule chooses facilities, severities, destinations, and associated forwarders. A severity threshold includes that severity and more serious levels; debug is more verbose than error. A facility mismatch can silently exclude an otherwise well-formed message. Distinguish the Syslog severity used by collection filtering from a security product’s own event severity field. If the same facility is collected through overlapping Syslog and CEF rules, investigate duplicate collection and separate the selections where needed. Reducing noise is useful only if you can show that required firewall or authentication events still arrive.

sections.title: Troubleshoot with evidence from each hop
sections.body: Begin at the appliance: confirm output format, destination, and a recent event. On the forwarder, confirm network arrival, daemon handling, and valid CEF syntax when using that connector. Check pipe delimiters and required escaping in CEF headers and extension values. Next inspect AMA operation, the DCR association, filtering, and destination workspace. Finally query the expected table by a narrow time range and host or vendor. If Syslog arrives but parsed CEF fields do not, focus on format and connector routing before rebuilding the whole agent. Keep troubleshooting changes temporary and return filters to the required scope.

remember: CEF via AMA normally populates CommonSecurityLog; Syslog via AMA populates Syslog.
Appliance → Linux daemon → AMA → workspace are separate checkpoints.
Facility and severity filters must include the actual source messages.
Avoid overlapping rules that ingest the same traffic twice.
pitfalls: CEF event severity and Syslog transport severity are different fields.
A listening forwarder does not prove AMA can reach Azure.

title: Azure diagnostics and custom log ingestion
subtitle: Use policy for scale and DCR-based schemas for custom events.
intro: A cloud resource can exist without its security-relevant logs appearing in Sentinel. Azure Activity captures management operations, resource logs capture service-specific operations, and custom applications may require a dedicated ingestion path. SC-200 scenarios ask you to choose the right mechanism, deploy it consistently, and troubleshoot the missing link. Understand the distinction between a diagnostic setting and an agent rule, and between a table definition and the API that supplies rows. For custom ingestion, think of the DCR as a contract: incoming stream schema, optional transformation, destination workspace, and output table must agree. Correct authentication alone cannot repair an incompatible schema.

sections.title: Separate control plane from data plane
sections.body: Azure Activity records management-plane operations such as resource creation and configuration changes. Export the relevant subscription activity through diagnostic settings to the Sentinel workspace and query AzureActivity. Resource logs describe operations inside a service, such as a Key Vault secret access, and typically require that resource’s diagnostic settings. A subscription Activity log export does not automatically collect every resource’s data-plane audit stream. In a scenario, identify what the attacker actually did before selecting the source. Reading a secret and changing a vault’s resource configuration require different evidence even though both involve the same vault.

sections.title: Use Azure Policy for coverage at scale
sections.body: Diagnostic settings specify which log categories or category groups are sent to destinations such as Log Analytics, Event Hubs, or Storage. Azure Policy can enforce or deploy appropriate settings across many resources or subscriptions. A deployIfNotExists assignment uses its managed identity and required permissions; existing noncompliant resources can require a remediation task. Scope the policy to the intended environment and verify the destination workspace parameter. Policy compliance means the expected configuration exists, so still verify fresh records. A mistaken workspace selection can produce an apparently healthy deployment while the SOC continues querying a different workspace.

sections.title: Define the custom ingestion contract
sections.body: Create a custom table with the required column names and types, including TimeGenerated. Custom table names use the _CL suffix. A DCR stream declaration describes the incoming shape; a data flow selects that stream, applies any supported transformation, and sends the transformed output to a destination. The output stream names the target table. Use the DCR ingestion endpoint or a data collection endpoint as required by the current architecture, including private-link requirements. An Entra application sending through the Logs Ingestion API needs authorized access to the DCR; this is not the same as possessing a workspace shared key.

sections.title: Transform and validate before activation
sections.body: Use an ingestion transformation to parse, rename, cast, or filter supported incoming data so the output matches the destination schema. The transformation uses the source input, and its output must include the required columns in their expected types. Verify the DCR immutable identifier and stream name used by the client, its token audience and role assignment, network reachability, and returned error details. Then query a known test event in the custom table. A successful HTTP submission is one checkpoint; inspect the row’s timestamp, parsed fields, and workspace before allowing detections to depend on it.

remember: AzureActivity is control-plane evidence; resource logs capture service-specific data-plane events.
Policy can deploy diagnostic settings; existing resources may need remediation.
DCR stream schema, transformation output, destination, and table schema must agree.
Logs Ingestion API uses Entra authorization on the DCR.
pitfalls: A custom table definition does not itself ingest any rows.
Activity log export does not replace Key Vault resource audit logging.
A DCR immutable ID is different from a workspace ID.

title: Threat intelligence ingestion and matching
subtitle: Bring in relevant indicators, manage their lifecycle, and correlate them with observed activity.
intro: Threat intelligence is useful when a trustworthy claim about an observable can be connected to activity in your environment. Ingesting a feed is only the first step. You must understand its format, delivery mechanism, freshness, confidence, and coverage, then choose a matching or enrichment workflow. SC-200 scenarios can distinguish TAXII collection from a custom upload API, one-time bulk import from ongoing synchronization, and an intelligence object from a confirmed compromise. Current Sentinel uses ThreatIntelIndicators and ThreatIntelObjects, so recognize legacy ThreatIntelligenceIndicator examples without assuming that an old schema is the correct place to troubleshoot a new integration.

sections.title: Choose an import method
sections.body: STIX structures threat intelligence; TAXII transports it between compatible systems. Use Sentinel’s TAXII connector when a provider offers a supported TAXII server and collection. Obtain the API root, collection identifier, and required credentials. A TIP or custom service can submit STIX objects through the upload API without requiring a data connector. A file import can add a prepared CSV or JSON set in bulk, with explicit handling of invalid entries. Choose based on the provider’s capability and the refresh requirement. A one-time file upload does not create a continuously maintained subscription to a vendor feed.

sections.title: Preserve intelligence context and lifecycle
sections.body: An indicator can contain an IP, domain, URL, or file hash plus validity, confidence, description, and source context. These attributes determine whether a match deserves urgent investigation. An expired or revoked indicator should not be treated like an active high-confidence threat. Review the latest version and use current lifecycle fields in queries. Threat actors, campaigns, attack patterns, and relationships are richer STIX objects rather than simple observable lists. Linking those objects can explain why a domain is interesting, but a relationship in intelligence is still not proof that a local account or device was compromised.

sections.title: Use the current tables and schema
sections.body: ThreatIntelIndicators holds indicator data, while ThreatIntelObjects supports broader STIX intelligence objects. Current management and hunting experiences use these schemas. Older content may query ThreatIntelligenceIndicator, so inspect and migrate the query rather than assuming an empty legacy table means ingestion failed. Field structures differ and may contain dynamic STIX data. Inspect sample records, extract typed fields, select the latest version of an object where appropriate, and preserve provenance. If a query joins IP indicators to network telemetry, ensure that both sides represent the same address meaning and use compatible types before interpreting the result.

sections.title: Turn intelligence into detection and enrichment
sections.body: A threat indicator match can raise an alert when a configured analytics rule correlates an active observable with local logs. The required telemetry must exist; importing a malicious IP does not produce a firewall connection event. Use supported threat-intelligence rules or carefully tested custom matches, map entities, and include useful evidence. Enrichment playbooks can retrieve additional context during triage without changing the underlying detection. Reduce low-value indicators through source selection and ingestion controls, then validate known test observables. The operational goal is a defensible investigation lead with source, time, and entity context, rather than the largest possible feed.

remember: STIX describes intelligence; TAXII is a transfer protocol.
The upload API can ingest STIX without a data connector.
Current intelligence queries use ThreatIntelIndicators and ThreatIntelObjects.
A match requires relevant local telemetry and valid indicator lifecycle handling.
pitfalls: An intelligence hit is an investigation lead, not automatic proof of compromise.
Bulk file import does not continuously synchronize the source.
Do not troubleshoot a new feed only through a legacy table name.

Delete all domain logs to reduce future matches.
Treat every expired indicator as currently malicious forever.
explanations: A match without lifecycle and contextual validation can be misleading.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate indicator quality and context rather than treating every hit equally.

title: Analytics, Data Lake, XDR retention, and table plans
subtitle: Keep operational detections fast while preserving the history investigators need.
intro: Retention questions combine three decisions: how data enters the platform, how long it remains available to operational analytics, and how long it is retained overall. The lowest storage price is not useful if a required real-time detection stops working. Current SC-200 explicitly includes Analytics, Data Lake, and XDR tiers, while Log Analytics table plans remain relevant to existing tables and older scenarios. Distinguish these settings instead of using “retention” as one undifferentiated number. A good design states which tables support active detections, which support historical forensics, and how analysts will access records after they leave the interactive period.

sections.title: Separate analytics retention from total retention
sections.body: Analytics retention is the period during which a table’s operational data remains available for the normal real-time SIEM experience. Total retention includes the historical period kept beyond it. In the current Sentinel platform, analytics data is mirrored into the lake, and total retention can extend the historical horizon. For a table that needs a recent investigation window and several years of evidence, configure both values deliberately. Increasing retention cannot resurrect data already removed. Before shortening it, evaluate investigation, compliance, and downstream detection dependencies; a cost-only change can eliminate evidence that the organization still needs.

sections.title: Choose the tier for the use case
sections.body: Keep data required by real-time analytics rules, operational hunting, and Sentinel dashboards in the Analytics tier. Use Data Lake for lower-touch history and supported lake queries, scheduled jobs, notebooks, and summarized analysis. Moving a table to lake-only storage affects real-time features that depended on that table. If only a small portion needs immediate analysis, assess supported filtering or split capabilities rather than blindly treating every row identically. Write down the exact consumer before changing a tier: an overnight historical trend job and an incident alert with a short response target have different requirements.

sections.title: Understand XDR’s default window and extension
sections.body: Defender XDR hunting data has a default 30-day window. Supported XDR tables can be ingested into Sentinel for longer Analytics or Data Lake retention, with ingestion and possible storage or processing charges depending on the chosen design. Extending a supported table beyond the default is a data-management operation, not simply a change to the hunting query’s time picker. Some XDR tables remain view-only for retention management in the portal, so check table support. Preserve the default XDR window as a distinct concept from Sentinel retention and verify licensing and cost implications before relying on older history.

sections.title: Keep table-plan terminology precise
sections.body: Log Analytics exposes Analytics, Basic, and Auxiliary/Lake table plans, whose supported tables, billing, querying, and operational features differ. Sentinel’s current centralized tier-management experience is related but is not just a synonym for every older table-plan setting. For example, Basic tables can be visible in the Defender portal while their configuration still requires Log Analytics; current documentation describes changing eligible tables to Analytics for centralized management. Check the exact table’s capabilities instead of assuming every low-cost plan has identical limitations. Validate both a historical query and a detection after a retention or plan change.

remember: Analytics retention and total retention answer different questions.
Lake-only data is not a drop-in replacement for real-time analytics-rule input.
Defender XDR’s default hunting window is 30 days; supported extension can incur Sentinel costs.
Check table eligibility and portal-specific management support before changing plans.
pitfalls: Extending retention cannot recover records already deleted.
A longer query time range does not provision a longer retention window.
Do not conflate Azure Monitor table plans with every Sentinel data-tier setting.

questions.stem: An analyst selects a 120-day range for an XDR table that has only its default hunting retention. No older records appear. What is the best explanation?
options: The time picker automatically buys historical storage but requires a browser refresh.

questions.stem: A team increases total retention today after old records have already been removed. Which expectation is correct?
options: The increased period restores all previously deleted rows.

title: Workbooks and SOC optimization
subtitle: Build useful operational views and improve the value of ingested telemetry.
intro: A workbook answers an operational question through queries and visual elements. It is not an ingestion pipeline, detection engine, or immutable copy of the data it displays. SOC optimization adds recommendations about underused data and detection coverage, but analysts must evaluate the business purpose and dependencies before acting. SC-200 can test the difference between saving a template and having the right data, between permission to open a workbook and permission to query its sources, and between cutting cost and improving security value. Practice explaining which query, parameter, table, and role support each chart so that an attractive visualization remains operationally trustworthy.

sections.title: Create and customize a useful workbook
sections.body: Install a solution or standalone workbook template from Content hub, verify its required data types, and save a workbook resource before customizing it. A workbook stores its definition, queries, parameters, and layout; saving it does not copy the underlying logs into that Azure resource. Choose tables and visualizations that answer a specific question, such as failed sign-ins by location over a selected interval. Build parameters for time, workspace, account, or device as needed. Use appropriate normalization where practical so a view is less dependent on one vendor’s raw schema.

sections.title: Treat queries and permissions as dependencies
sections.body: Workbook access and access to the queried data are separate requirements. An analyst may open a saved workbook yet see errors or empty results because the workspace, table, or external source is unavailable to that identity. Test as the intended reader, not only as the author. Filter early, use an appropriate time range, and summarize to the granularity needed by the chart. A parameter should actually bind to each relevant query; changing a displayed time label alone cannot alter a hardcoded query window. Validate numbers against a direct query before reporting trends to leadership.

sections.title: Use recommendations to improve coverage
sections.body: SOC optimization can identify missing detections for ingested sources, missing sources for useful detections, and opportunities to improve the value of costly data. Treat a recommendation as a starting point for an engineering decision. If useful authentication data has no active detections, enabling and tuning relevant templates might improve coverage more than stopping collection. If a required source is missing, a rule alone cannot solve the gap. Review the stated threat, required telemetry, current coverage, and recommended actions. Track completion and confirm the intended protection after implementing the change.

sections.title: Optimize cost without losing evidence
sections.body: Unused or lightly used tables can signal opportunities to adjust ingestion, plans, retention, or detection content. However, query usage is not the only measure of business value. Compliance evidence and rare incident investigations can justify retaining data that analysts seldom open. Consider ingestion volume, dependencies, investigation needs, and commitment-tier fit together. Establish a baseline, change one well-understood setting, and compare costs and detection health afterward. A smaller bill paired with a blind spot is not a successful optimization. Workbooks and table insights can help show whether ingestion and security outcomes changed as intended.

remember: A saved workbook stores its definition, not a separate log archive.
Workbook visibility does not automatically grant access to every data source.
Optimization recommendations can improve detections as well as reduce cost.
Validate compliance and investigation requirements before stopping ingestion.
pitfalls: A workbook’s empty chart does not prove the source generated no events.
A data-value recommendation is not permission to delete required evidence.

options: Stop ingestion immediately because no rule currently reads it.
Review relevant rule templates, enable and tune suitable detections, and verify the resulting coverage.
Assume the recommendation means Microsoft found no security value in authentication logs.
Replace the table with a screenshot of its daily count.

Correct. Data-value optimization can mean improving the security use of an existing source.
Low current use is not a judgment that a source cannot be valuable.

questions.stem: A rarely queried table is required for regulatory evidence and occasional historical investigations. An optimization suggests reducing its cost. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Delete it because recent query frequency is low.

Keep only its workbook title.
Disable all related data-source audit settings without review.

A title does not preserve event evidence.
Stopping source auditing can destroy the required future record.

title: Sentinel analytics rules and detection scheduling
subtitle: Choose scheduled or NRT execution, map entities, and handle latency and grouping.
intro: A good detection is more than a query that once returned an interesting row. It must run at an appropriate cadence, evaluate the right time window, produce useful entities and evidence, and create manageable incidents. Sentinel supports scheduled, near-real-time, threat-intelligence, and machine-learning-related detection experiences; current Microsoft guidance also promotes unified custom detections across the Defender portal. SC-200 still expects the Sentinel analytics distinctions in its published objectives. Learn the operational meaning of frequency, lookback, threshold, grouping, and suppression. Then use those controls to explain why a scenario misses delayed events, repeats alerts, or produces an incident with weak investigation context.

sections.title: Choose the execution model
sections.body: Scheduled rules run a KQL query at a configurable frequency over a defined lookback window. NRT rules run frequently using ingestion-time handling to detect suitable recently ingested events with low latency. NRT is not simply a scheduled rule whose interval an author types as one minute, and supported query behavior must be checked against current documentation. Threat-intelligence matching correlates observable intelligence with local activity. Machine-learning and correlation features combine signals differently from a deterministic threshold query. Choose the model based on detection latency, source arrival patterns, required query logic, and available telemetry rather than assuming faster is always better.

sections.title: Keep frequency and lookback distinct
sections.body: Frequency answers how often the query runs. Lookback answers how much event history that execution evaluates. The interval must not exceed the lookback, because that creates gaps. Overlap can help accommodate correlation windows but can also repeat results unless the logic accounts for it. Scheduled rules have built-in scheduling delay, yet sources may arrive later than that allowance. Measure ingestion delay and design a sufficiently broad event window with an appropriate ingestion-time boundary to avoid both missed and repeated results. Do not hardcode an overly narrow time filter inside a query that defeats the intended rule lookback.

sections.title: Produce alerts that support investigation
sections.body: Entity mapping identifies meaningful accounts, hosts, IPs, and other assets from returned fields; use strong identifiers where possible. Custom details preserve additional context, while alert-detail overrides can make titles and severity useful for the returned activity. The alert threshold evaluates the query results, so understand whether each row is an event or an aggregate before selecting a count threshold. Event grouping determines whether results become one alert or separate alerts. Incident grouping governs how alerts are collected into incidents, subject to the portal’s correlation behavior. These controls act at different stages and should be tested independently.

sections.title: Validate and operate the detection
sections.body: Start from supported templates where practical, inspect required sources, run the query over representative data, and test expected matches and benign activity. Use simulation and preview features where available. After activation, monitor execution health, errors, data volume, latency, alert quality, and coverage. Suppression temporarily stops rule execution after a match; it is not the same as grouping related alerts or narrowly excluding a known benign entity in the query. If onboarding to the Defender portal changes incident correlation, evaluate the resulting incidents there rather than assuming every legacy grouping behavior remains identical.

remember: Frequency is cadence; lookback is evaluated history.
A query interval longer than lookback leaves uncovered time.
Entity mapping and custom details enrich alerts; grouping controls alert/incident packaging.
NRT uses ingestion-time logic and has its own supported behavior.
pitfalls: Suppression can hide later genuine activity while the rule is paused.
A threshold on aggregate rows is not automatically a threshold on underlying events.
Source latency can exceed the built-in scheduling allowance.

Explain its frequency, lookback, threshold, and entity mappings.
Compare TimeGenerated with ingestion_time() for sample records.

options: Frequency 1 hour; lookback 15 minutes.
Frequency 15 minutes; lookback 1 hour.
Frequency 1 day; lookback 1 minute.
Frequency and lookback both mean the same setting.

Correct. The cadence is 15 minutes, while each run considers an hour of history.

questions.takeaway: Read frequency and lookback as separate clocks.

questions.stem: A query matches expected activity but its alerts have poor investigation context. Choose TWO changes that directly improve alert content without changing the matching condition.
options: Map returned strong account, host, or IP identifiers to entities.
Add relevant returned evidence as custom details or alert-detail overrides.
Remove all returned identifiers after aggregation.
Set the query interval longer than its lookback.
explanations: Correct. Entity mapping enables meaningful investigation pivots.
Correct. Useful alert fields and custom details carry context into triage.

questions.takeaway: Enrichment makes a valid detection operationally useful.

questions.stem: A log source often arrives 20 minutes after event generation. A scheduled rule only looks back five minutes by event time and misses those events. What is the best design response?
options: Expand the event-time window based on measured delay and use suitable ingestion-time logic to control repeated processing.
Increase only the alert severity.
Change the rule title to “late events.”
Assume the built-in scheduled-rule delay handles every possible source delay.
explanations: Correct. The timing design must include events that arrive later than the original event-time window.
Severity changes prioritization, not which events are evaluated.
A title cannot alter timing or query selection.
Built-in delay is not a guarantee against arbitrary upstream latency.
questions.takeaway: Measure and design for the source’s actual ingestion delay.

questions.stem: A detection produces repeated benign matches from one documented maintenance account. The team proposes pausing the entire rule for a day after any alert. What is the principal concern?
options: Suppression pauses execution and could miss a real attack by another account during that period.
Suppression only changes the alert title.
Suppression is identical to entity mapping.
Suppression automatically proves the maintenance account is safe forever.
explanations: Correct. A narrow, validated exclusion or other tuning may better preserve unrelated detection coverage.
Suppression affects execution, not merely presentation.
Mapping identifies assets and does not pause detection.
A tuning control does not establish permanent trust in an account.
questions.takeaway: Understand the coverage cost of broad suppression.
